Jesus didn't come to tell us to 'look inward' for a vibration; He came to be the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world.  
>   
> In Daniel 7:14, the Son of Man is given an authority that is absolute and eternal—it isn't something we 'cultivate' by thought; it is a reality we must submit to. God is indeed Love, but He is also Just. Without the King of Kings holding the keys to death and Hades (Rev 1:18), our 'inward love' has no power over the grave. Claiming we don't need a Messiah isn't 'tangible evidence'—it's the ultimate pride of the soul, and it’s a dangerous foundation to build an eternity on.

> The Gnostic gospels like Thomas, Judas, and Philip are not controversial texts that were excluded because they were too deep. They are late documents, mostly from the second to fourth centuries, written long after Jesus and not by the people whose names they claim. That is the consensus view of historians across the board, including secular and atheist scholars.  
>   
> We know this because they do not fit the first century Jewish world Jesus lived in. Their theology reflects later Greek philosophical ideas such as dualism and secret knowledge rather than Jewish covenant thinking. They also contain clear anachronisms. The language, concepts, and assumptions simply do not belong to the time or place they describe. In several cases they even get basic historical and cultural details wrong, including names common to the period, practices in Judea, and imagery that does not match the region or era. That is how historians date texts. When details repeatedly miss their setting, the author is writing later and projecting ideas backward.  
>   
> By contrast, the canonical gospels are first century texts tied to early eyewitness communities and deeply embedded in Jewish thought. That is why they present the Kingdom of God as God’s reign breaking into history rather than private enlightenment or self divinisation.  
>   
> Even the phrase “the kingdom of God is within you” is not uniquely Gnostic. In the Greek it more accurately means “in your midst,” referring to God’s reign present through Jesus himself, not humans becoming their own gods. >   
> • Matthew 5:17 says “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law of the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them.”  
>   
> • In Matthew 19:4-5 and Mark 10:6-8 Jesus directly quotes Genesis 1:27 and Genesis 2:24.   
>   
> • Jesus talks about David in Mark 2:25-26 and Matthew 22:41-46.  
>   
> • John 8:58 says “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am” so not only does Jesus talk about Yahweh, he claims to be Yahweh.

>

And when he finds it, he joyfully puts it on his shoulders and goes home. Then he calls his friends and neighbors together and says, ‘Rejoice with me; I have found my lost sheep.’ I tell you that in the same way there will be more rejoicing in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need to repent."  
>   
> • The whole point of the parable is that the lost sheep is "lost" because it is not following God. That's the whole reason the shepherd (God) goes after it in the first place, to bring it back, and when it returns, it pleases God.

Thank you, Prof. Jian, for this incredibly interesting lecture. 

I truly appreciated your interpretation of Dante's verses in Chapter VII of the Divine Comedy, as it resonnates with my interpretation made in a short essay, which I'm pasting below.

Dante reflects on the crucifixion of Christ as the ultimate divine act of love—a love so profound that it encompasses both justice and mercy in perfect harmony. As Dante writes, “God chose to act with both mercy and justice at once: on one hand, offering Himself to suffer and die for us in an act of infinite mercy; on the other, through this passion and death providing the only adequate sacrifice to fully atone for human guilt—an act of supreme justice.” This union of unyielding rigor with supernatural compassion is unparalleled in all human history and will remain unmatched for eternity.


Dante reminds us that such a decree lies beyond human comprehension unless one’s intellect is fully matured in the flame of divine love: “This decree, brother, is buried from the eyes of all whose intellect has not grown in the flame of love.” The crucifixion reveals a paradox that humanity can never fully apprehend—a divine act where justice and forgiveness are not opposites but facets of a single truth. It is this ineffable union that makes divine love both awe-inspiring and humbling.

According to a passage found in Josephus' Antiquities of the Jews (20.9.1), "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James" met his death after the death of the procurator Porcius Festus but before Lucceius Albinus had assumed office – which has been dated to 62.[100] The High Priest Hanan ben Hanan (Ananus ben Ananus) took advantage of this lack of imperial oversight to assemble a Sanhedrin (literally a synhedrion kriton in Greek, a "Sanhedrin of judges"), which condemned James "on the charge of breaking the law", then had him executed by stoning (Antiquities 20.9.1). Josephus reports that Hanan's act was widely viewed as little more than judicial murder and offended a number of "those who were considered the most fair-minded people in the city, and strict in their observance of the Law", who went so far as to arrange a meeting with Albinus as he entered the province in order to petition him successfully about the matter. In response, King Agrippa II replaced Ananus with Jesus son of Damneus.[101]

Nice lecture and i like Professor Jiang 
BUT 
in this lecture there are some inaccuracies, for example Jesus “attacked the Romans,” but that isn’t what the Gospels actually describe. Scripture shows that Jesus rarely confronted Roman authority. Instead, His strongest criticisms were aimed at the religious leadership of His own time specifically the Pharisees, the scribes, and the Temple establishment. Passages make it clear that His mission wasn’t a political rebellion against Rome, but a spiritual challenge to the religious hypocrisy and corruption within His own community.

I mention this only because it’s important to stay close to what the text actually says not the simplified version that sometimes gets repeated.

Also, this wasn’t about all Jewish people Jesus himself was Jewish, but his message of spiritual renewal and moral accountability put pressure on the Jews in positions of power, which is why they reacted so strongly as to kill him.

To steel man the Christian tradition, it's not necessarily about "not asking questions." Christianity has a long history of theological inquiry, wherein many questions are asked, with attempts to answer them. Christianity is a large religion with many sects, and many of them do not ascribe to the idea that faith requires a suspension of reason. "Israelite," of course, means "one who wrestles with God." It is also worth noting that the "mysteries" you struggle with in this video, particularly the ressurection, have deep emotional significance. He resurrects as one who conquers death, turning the cross into the very symbol of redemption. They are mysteries insofar as they are divine occurrences, and the divine is beyond our egocentric understanding or fragile intellect. Their being mysteries doesn't preclude them from being meaningful, or having both obvious and subtle meanings that God wishes us to ascertain, but it does preclude them from being understood to their fullness. That would require the mind of God, of which our individual "divine spark" is merely a minute manifestation.

### **@oscarsantiagonorenahemelbe4396** | 👍 30 likes
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pp0E1gb80WQ&lc=UgzMqvkBbyqGCuQuDUh4AaABAg)

I watched the whole lecture, and I actually appreciated it because it made me think.

The issue isn’t that Jesus is discussed or even questioned in school that’s normal in education. The problem is how it’s presented. A fair class would say: “Here is the traditional Christian interpretation, and here are alternative academic interpretations.”
But the lecture presents one philosophical view as established history while portraying Christian belief as naive.

Several points are not scholarly consensus:

• Christianity is reduced to “believe or go to hell” (02:53) official doctrine actually teaches that people who never knew Christ without fault and sincerely seek truth can be saved (Catechism 847).
• Faith is described as “don’t question” (04:11) historically Christianity produced thinkers like Augustine and Aquinas precisely because believers tried to reason about faith.
• “We only know four facts about Jesus” (05:05) historians agree on more (preaching in Galilee, disciples, crucifixion under Pilate, continuation of the movement — Britannica).
• Gospel of Thomas as the original teaching (33:02) usually dated to the 2nd century, later than the canonical Gospels.
• Reincarnation and multiple lifetimes (1:35:15) this is a philosophical belief, not something taught in 1st-century Judaism, and Jesus was Jewish.

So, the video contains real historical elements, but mixes history with personal philosophy and presents it as academic consensus.

I don’t think the professor is malicious he likely believes his interpretation, but the lecture is not neutral history. It proposes a different Jesus, closer to a modern gnostic/new-age reading.

Ironically, it strengthened my faith.
Questions don’t destroy faith caricatures and half-truths do.

Prof. Jiang presents an interesting philosophical narrative, but historically this lecture mixes Gnosticism, Neoplatonism, Dostoevsky, and modern anti-Catholic tropes with first-century history without proper methodological control.

A few major issues:

The Gospel of Thomas (Nag Hammadi, discovered 1945) is a 2nd-century Gnostic text. Most scholars date it 120–150 CE. It cannot simply be assumed to preserve the “true” teachings of Jesus over earlier sources like Mark (~70 CE) or Paul (~50 CE).

There is no serious historical evidence that the Romans invented Christianity. Early Christians were persecuted by Rome (e.g., Nero, 64 CE). If it was Roman propaganda, why execute its followers for 250 years?

The claim that the Gospels were written to shift blame from Rome to Jews oversimplifies Second Temple Jewish intra-community conflict. The polemics reflect internal Jewish debates, not Roman authorship.

Reincarnation and “divine spark monad cosmology” are foreign to first-century Palestinian Judaism. Jesus operated within apocalyptic Jewish eschatology, not Platonic metaphysics.

Using Dostoevsky’s Grand Inquisitor as historical explanation is philosophically creative but not historiographically valid.

One can critique institutional Christianity, but that must be done using first-century sources, textual criticism, and Second Temple context — not later Gnostic speculation.

Important discussion, but it needs sharper historical methodology.

> The Pseudo-Clementines: Early Christian writings (3rd century) that record debates between Peter and the "disciples of John," showing that John's followers were still a competing group centuries later.

Just finished reading Dante again. This must be the eighth or ninth time in my life that I've come back to this text, and I really think it's the greatest work of art I've ever encountered. (To say nothing of Walking with Dante by Mark Scarbrough, the best podcast and best literary analysis I've ever encountered. Give it a listen!) Finally wrote down some thoughts on why so I can more effectively bother my friends about it: 
It’s the greatest work of Western Literature, whatever the hell that means. It’s the peak of what all western lit tries to accomplish. It’s a complete political, philosophical, and scientific treatise by a middle-aged ex-city counselor who was overthrown in a coup, sentenced to death in absentia, and spent the last 20 years of his life in exile. It's the world's greatest self-insert fanfiction, the tale of the author's favorite ancient poet and Dead Childhood Crush giving him a guided tour of the known universe, where most of his enemies are in hell and every saint, sinner, conqueror, poet, and pagan who ever lived says "wow Dante you're so cool. One of us fr fr, only built different." It’s a thrilling, accessible adventure story on the surface. Underneath, it’s the most intricately crafted work of art I’ve ever seen, packed with insane numerology, multiple levels of allegory, references to every last classical, biblical, medieval, or contemporary source this poet on the run could get his hands on, calls back and forth across cantos and themes, and exquisite wordplay, all layered over incredibly tight and complex rhyme and rhythm schemes that must have given him ulcers.
It’s a universal text of all creation that lays out full doctrines of theology, philosophy, politics, history, art, literature, and every feeling and state of the human heart or natural world. It’s deeply personal and comically petty, running down into denunciations of Dante’s political enemies, hall-of-fame hornyposting about his Dead Childhood Crush, racist jokes dunking on every other subspecies of Italian, and somber meditations on the bitter pill of exile. It will jump straight from the most beautiful nine-layer metaphor you’ve ever heard to a fourth-grade joke about demons farting or losing their erections. 
It's flawless and self-referential in ways I didn't even think possible, and it's loaded with all the dumb errors and typos of parchment writing on the run. It’s the supreme self-righteousness of a man who believed he was the best Catholic to ever live, and it’s shockingly heretical. Running underneath it all is this absolutely revolutionary thesis that worldly wisdom, art, and even and especially sexual desire are paths to the divine. It’s the sum of ancient learning, the peak of medieval art, and the dawn of the modern spirit. All life is in the Comedy.

### **@c.f.p** | 👍 2 likes

📌1. At 4:10 he says “How did Jesus die for our sins? Why is there a second coming? It’s all a miracle. Meaning don’t question it. Just believe in it.” 

• This presupposes a materialistic worldview. But if God designed and created the universe (i.e., if God is the author of the laws of nature), a miracle can easily be explained as God himself intervening from the outside. John Lennox (professor and mathematician) explains this. 

• Furthermore, the Bible teaches the opposite of “not questioning it”. 1 Corinthians 15:14-19 says “And if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is useless and so is your faith.”

------------------------------------

📌2. At 14:41 he says that the Bible’s portrayal of the Pharisees conspiring with the Roman authorities to arrest Jesus could not have happened because “within the Jewish tradition it’s ok to argue.”

• The Bible does not say that Jesus was arrested for “arguing” it says that he was arrested for claiming to be God (i.e., blasphemy). John 19:6-7 says “As soon as the chief priests and their officials saw him, they shouted, ‘Crucify! Crucify!’ But Pilate answered, ‘You take him and crucify him. As for me, I find no basis for a charge against him.’ The Jewish leaders insisted, ‘We have a law, and according to that law he must die, because he claimed to be the Son of God.’

------------------------------------

📌3. At 37:09 he says “So there’s no way Jesus would say ‘follow me and you’re good, believe in me and you’re good’. He would never ever say that because he knows you can’t follow someone else, you have to believe in yourself.”

• Matthew 16:24 (and similarly Luke 9:23) says “Then Jesus said to his disciples, ‘Whoever wants to be my disciple must deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me.’” So Jesus actually did teach self-denial and strict obedience to God.

------------------------------------

📌4. At 37:51 he says “Throughout the gospel of Thomas he actually doesn’t refer to the bible, he doesn’t talk about Adam and Eve, he doesn’t talk about Yahweh, he doesn’t talk about David, he doesn’t talk about Moses, because for him it’s all fake.”

• The Gospel of Thomas is non-canonical for many good reasons (e.g., lack of a narrative, alleged late composition and probable forgery, theological discrepancies, etc). Wesley Huff @WesHuff (theologian) has videos on this). 

• The claim that “he doesn’t talk about (…) because for him it’s all fake” is directly contradicted in the canonical gospels:

• John 5:46 says “If you believed in Moses, you would believe in me, for he wrote about me.”

• Matthew 5:17 says “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law of the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them.”

• In Matthew 19:4-5 and Mark 10:6-8 Jesus directly quotes Genesis 1:27 and Genesis 2:24. 

• Jesus talks about David in Mark 2:25-26 and Matthew 22:41-46.

• John 8:58 says “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am” so not only does Jesus talk about Yahweh, he claims to be Yahweh. 

------------------------------------

📌5. Jesus never said “be yourself” he said the exact opposite (i.e., to deny yourself) Matthew 16:24-26, Luke 9:23, and Galatians 2:20. 

------------------------------------

📌6. The question about Jesus being the Son of God and God himself has actually been answered in the Bible. The Bible explains that God entered his own creation (i.e., God entered the material universe) as a man, Jesus (i.e., God in human form). John 1:1 and John 1:14.

------------------------------------

📌7. At 1:57 he says “we disobeyed God and we ate from the tree of knowledge”. 

• It was the tree of knowledge of good and evil, not the tree of knowledge. Oxford Professor John Lennox has a brilliant clip addressing this.

------------------------------------

📌8. At 47:36 he says that the message of the "The Parable of the Lost Sheep" is that "God doesn't want obedience" and that he cares more for people who are disobedient "than he cares for those who obey him because those who obey him contribute nothing to the universe."
 
• The message of "The Parable of the Lost Sheep" is that God seeks out the sinner and rejoices when they are found. 

Luke 15:4-7 says "Suppose one of you has a hundred sheep and loses one of them. Doesn’t he leave the ninety-nine in the open country and go after the lost sheep until he finds it? And when he finds it, he joyfully puts it on his shoulders and goes home. Then he calls his friends and neighbors together and says, ‘Rejoice with me; I have found my lost sheep.’ I tell you that in the same way there will be more rejoicing in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need to repent."

• The whole point of the parable is that the lost sheep is "lost" because it is not following God. That's the whole reason the shepherd (God) goes after it in the first place, to bring it back, and when it returns, it pleases God.

------------------------------------

📌9. At 50:12 he says that "The Parable of the Great Banquet" is that "the worst people in the world are the rich people." 

• The message of "The Parable of the Great Banquet" is that Jesus invited his own people (the Jewish nation) to the banquet (i.e., invited them to the kingdom), but the invitation was rejected and so the invitation was extended to the Gentiles. Meaning that grace is a gift of God for all who are willing to come regardless of their heritage.

------------------------------------

📌 10. At 51:56 he says to "listen to your heart" and do what you enjoy because it will connect you to the divine

• Jeremiah 17:9 says "The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure."

• Matthew 26:41 says "Watch and pray so that you will not fall into temptation. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak."

------------------------------------

📌 11. At 56:09 he says that Dostoevsky believed that Jesus said that "freedom is what will enable us to seek the divine".

• Dostoevsky was an Orthodox Christian, so he wasn't celebrating freedom for the sake of celebrating freedom. He believed that freedom was the necessary prerequisite for genuine love. In other words, he believed that in order to be real, love has to be free. In other words, God gave us free will because he desires a relationship based on voluntary love, that we may choose to FOLLOW him willingly. So freedom is not the goal. Freedom is the necessary condition that gives meaning to our choice to follow God.

------------------------------------

📌 12. At 56:37 he says that Satan wants us to obey authority and Jesus wants us to obey ourselves. That is completely twisted. 

• Genesis 3:5 says that Satan tells mankind that they can be like God. That is why Satanists don't worship Satan, they worship themselves (they believe that the individual is the highest authority and that each person is his own God).

------------------------------------

📌 13. At 58:29 he implies that Dostoevsky believed that Jesus taught that "People want to obey. People want to be told what to do.".

• Jesus taught that people do NOT want to obey and they do NOT want to be told what to do. That instead, they want to follow their own hearts and their own desires. 

 ------------------------------------

📌 14. At 1:10:46 he says "The Catholic Church teaches you that Jesus redeemed us from our sins. But then the question is, why did Jesus have to kill himself again? That makes no sense."

• The answer is in Romans 6:23 "For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord."

------------------------------------

📌15. At 1:18:20 he says that God entered the world as Jesus to physically punish himself so that we feel bad and stop sinning. 

• That is a serious misinterpretation of the Gospel. It is not Christian doctrine that Jesus' sacrifice was intended to emotionally manipulate or guilt trip anyone. Jesus' sacrifice was the means by which God satisfied the legal requirement of the law (the law being that the wages of sin is death).

------------------------------------

📌 16. At 1:34:37 he says that the message of Matthew 7:21-23 is that "Jesus says 'Don't follow me, follow your heart". 

• The real meaning of Matthew 7:21-23 is that you shouldn't be Christian in name only. That you should actually practice what you preach.

------------------------------------

📌 17. At 1:36:00 he says "If your spark has been dimmed, it goes to a lower place." 

• That doesn't sound like Christian doctrine, that sounds like Buddhism and Hinduism.

     "and begged him to let the sick just touch the edge of his cloak, and all who touched it were healed."

and Jesus himself said we are capable of doing the same, even greater things in John 14:12:

     “I tell you the truth, anyone who believes in me will do the same works I have done, and even greater works, because I am going to be with the Father."

5. Jesus didn't teach, "believe in me and you'll be saved."
He ABSOLUTELY did. John 14:6:

     "Jesus answered, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me."

If you can't get to the Father, that means you are not a child of God. John 1:10 (listed above) says we have the RIGHT to BECOME children of God. That's not how we start.

6. Why did the Romans kill Jesus?
Pilate was on thin ice with Rome and knew that if he screwed something up in Judea, he could be removed from power and replaced. The religious leaders had whipped the crowd up into a frenzy, saying things like John 19:12:

     "From then on, Pilate tried to set Jesus free, but the Jewish leaders kept shouting, “If you let this man go, you are no friend of Caesar. Anyone who claims to be a king opposes Caesar.”

7. What is Jesus's central message?
In a single verse, it is found in Matthew 22:36-40

     "36 “Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the Law?”



     "37 Jesus replied: “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’[a] 38 This is the first and greatest commandment. 39 And the second is like it: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’[b] 40 All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments.”

To love God is to love Jesus, which is found in John 14:21

     "21 Whoever has my commands and keeps them is the one who loves me. The one who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I too will love them and show myself to them.”

When we accept Christ's forgiveness for our sins, we are commanded to forgive our enemies lest we risk not being forgiven ourselves, as stated in Matthew 6:15:

     "But if you do not forgive others their sins, your Father will not forgive your sins."

8. Are the Romans excused from all blame?
No, as found in John 19:11 when Jesus is addressing Pilate after he was flogged:

     "Jesus answered, “You would have no power over me if it were not given to you from above. Therefore the one who handed me over to you is guilty of a greater sin.”

Jesus dying on the cross was always a part of God's plan to redeem humanity. If it wasn't Rome, it would have been whatever other empire could provide a reliable system of roads, very few common languages, and relative global peace required for the message to explode across the globe.

“Messiah” in that time meant different things to different people. Many expected a political or military leader who would overthrow Roman rule. ### **@kidmick809**
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pp0E1gb80WQ&lc=UgyMJCIWIBiwmSyfHFN4AaABAg)

Historians agree on some core facts about Jesus, like that he was a Jewish teacher and was crucified under Pontius Pilate. But saying we only know a few things for sure is misleading. When you look at the earliest sources, especially the letters of Paul the Apostle, there is more context than that.

Paul’s letters are usually dated to around 50–60 CE, just a couple of decades after Jesus’ death. He clearly treats Jesus as a real historical person who was crucified and already had an established following. He also says he met people like James the Just and Peter, which directly connects his writings to the earliest circle of followers.

The timeline of the Gospels matters too. The Gospel of Mark is generally dated around 70 CE, with Matthew and Luke around 80–90 CE, and John around 90–100 CE. These are the earliest narrative accounts of Jesus’ life and teachings.

The Gospel of Thomas, on the other hand, is not part of the New Testament and is usually dated later, around 120–140 CE or beyond. While it may preserve some early sayings, most scholars see it as reflecting a different theological perspective, not a more original version of Jesus’ message. Treating it as more reliable than earlier sources like Paul or Mark goes against how historians normally weigh evidence.

The discussion of responsibility for Jesus’ death is also oversimplified. Crucifixion was a Roman punishment carried out under Pontius Pilate. At the same time, Paul, who was a Pharisee, describes real conflict within Jewish communities, including persecution of early Christians. The situation is more complex than blaming one side.

The claim that James the Just was simply protected also leaves out key context. The historian Josephus reports that James was later executed, which shows a more complicated relationship between early Christians and Jewish authorities.

Finally, the lecture shifts from history into philosophy without making that clear. The idea that Jesus taught essentially the same message as figures like Plato or Zoroaster is not a mainstream historical conclusion, but a modern interpretation.

Overall, the lecture presents a selective view that downplays earlier sources like Paul and elevates later ones like the Gospel of Thomas, while presenting debated ideas as settled fact.

### **@hrjohansenskanal**
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pp0E1gb80WQ&lc=UgyYecOT2BsE4dMlNYN4AaABAg)

Jangs third point—“either believe in Jesus or burn in hell”—is an oversimplified strawman.

According to Scripture, the issue is deeper than a forced choice between two extremes. Every human being who has ever lived has transgressed God’s moral law. That is what the Bible means by calling us sinners—we are lawbreakers by nature. Because all are born with a tendency toward selfishness and sin, God cannot simply say, “Never mind, I will give everyone eternal life anyway.”

Why? Because if He did, sin—with all its consequences of suffering, conflict, and destruction—would arise again, even in heaven, just as we see it on earth.

Yet this is the tension: God desires to give us eternal life.

So what does He do?

He sends Jesus and accepting HIS death as a sacrifice for YOUR sins, it can produce a change in the heart, having a new sensitive conscience and start a process of sanctification where you put away your sinful habits and gradually develop a true Christlike character.

But here is the problem:

In the days of Noah, he warned thousands, if not millions of a soon coming catastrophic event and begged people to repent their sins and be saved. For 120 years Noah preached, but ONLY eight were saved. This shows that the issue is not HEARING or understanding who God is and understand His requirements. The problem is unwillingness to believe and respond in the RIGHT way!

So even among those who profess belief in the biblical God, the majority do not truly submit to God. Many desire religion and worship only in form, but not obedience in life. They may embrace symbols, traditions, and teachings, yet resist the transformation God requires to be saved.

So what about them who have never heard about Jesus or about the plan of salvation?

Scripture points to a group of none-believers (gentiles) who sincerely seek righteousness, who desire truth, moral purity, long for having a noble, honest character and integrity in their lives. Without knowing Jesus personally or in scripture they respond to the inner conviction of right and wrong because they respond to voice of the Holy Spirit in their conscience. 

Paul explains it in Romans 2, 14-15 (Amplified Bible Version):

“14 When Gentiles, who do not have the Law [since it was given only to Jews], do [c]instinctively the things the Law requires [guided only by their conscience], they are a law to themselves, though they do not have the Law. 15 They show that the essential requirements of the Law are written in their hearts; and their conscience [their sense of right and wrong, their moral choices] bearing witness and their thoughts alternately accusing or perhaps defending them…”

This means that even those without explicit knowledge of Christ or Gods moral law are NOT without light. The Spirit of Christ works on every human heart but ONLY a very few responds positively. 

So the decisive issue is therefore not exposure to INFORMATION, but response to that inner conviction in our hearts (conscience).

However, the sad reality is that most people—whether professed Christians, religious, secular, or atheists—choose to reject that voice consistently. When obedience conflicts with personal gain, comfort, or ambition, they turn away and violate their conscience. 

That is why the number of the saved—both among gentiles and professed Christians—is VERY small compared relative to the world population—when Jesus comes the second time.

This was true in Noah’s time, and Christ Himself says that it will be the same at His second coming: “But as the days of Noah were, so shall also the coming of the Son of man be.”

So the issue is not that God condemns those who has lack of knowledge but rather that people are lost because they repeatedly reject the light and opportunities to they do receive constantly —whether through Scripture or through the Holy Spirit in their conscience.

This isn't a vague philosophical idea—it is backed by over 300 specific Messianic prophecies written centuries before his birth, ranging from his lineage and birthplace to the exact manner of his execution (Psalm 22, Isaiah 53). Mathematicians have shown that the probability of one man fulfilling even eight of these is statistically impossible.

### **@hrjohansenskanal**
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pp0E1gb80WQ&lc=UgyQUBG63FNlkzFFqQp4AaABAg)

I have only listened a few minutes, and from this very beginning, professor Jang shows that his interpretation is built on a limited, largely secular understanding of Christianity. A simple example illustrates this: he refers to “the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” only as “the tree of knowledge.” While this may seem innocent and maybe not intentional, such omissions are often used to portray God as a tyrant—one who deliberately keeps humanity in ignorance and demands strict obedience while withholding then the truth.

It’s somewhat frustrating that someone who sets out to explain the reasons for believing in the biblical God reveals, from the very first sentences in the seminar, seem to have a limited grasp of the biblical text and is maybe even (unconsciously?) repeating secular preconceptions often used to strawman and attack Christianity . 

It’s somewhat frustrating that someone who sets out to explain the reasons for believing in the biblical God reveals, from the very first sentences, seem to have a maybe presumptuous and limited grasp of what the Bible actually teaches.

Jang also claims that it is “already confusing” that Christians believe that Jesus is both the Son of God and God at the same time.

A way to understand this is to recognize that the term “Son” in this context is not about origin or a lesser status, but about his special role, relationship. In biblical language, “sonship” frequently conveys chosenness, representation, and shared authority rather than literal derivation. For example, the people of Israel are referred to as God’s “firstborn,” which does not imply that they were (physically) generated by God, but that they were chosen for a unique purpose, role and inheritance.

In the same way, calling Jesus the “Son of God” expresses his unique relationship with the Father and his role in revealing and carrying out the plan of salvation..

With respect, Professor, your narrative that Jesus was merely a victim of Roman politics overlooks the primary theological conflict in the Gospels. The Jewish Sanhedrin sought his death specifically because of his claim to deity. Jesus referred to himself as the 'Son of Man' over 80 times, directly invoking Daniel 7:13–14. To the High Priest (Mark 14:62), this wasn't just a title—it was a claim to the divine authority of the Ancient of Days, which they considered blasphemy.
Even the extra-biblical texts you often cite, like 1 Enoch and 2 Esdras, describe the 'Son of Man' as a pre-existent, divine Judge of the universe. To ignore this is to miss the very core of his identity in the ancient world.
Furthermore, there is a heavy spiritual weight to leading 1.5 million people toward a 'Gnostic' or purely political Christ. The Apostles didn't just 'teach' these things; they sealed their testimony with their blood. Every single one of them (save for John) was horrifically martyred for refusing to recant the claim that Jesus is the Risen Son of Man with all authority. They were willing to take that claim to the grave because they knew it was the truth. Are you willing to stake your eternity on a theory that contradicts both the scriptures and the lives of those who walked with Him? The judgment for leading others astray is a heavy burden, and I hope you consider the weight of that reality.

### **@tajefleming810**
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pp0E1gb80WQ&lc=UgxAT1HYZ-fTbcnJf9B4AaABAg)

Respect, Professor for your work and your dedication to analysis thinking but you are wrong about Jesus. 

Your bible interpretation is a misinterpretation. 

Jesus is both the Son of God and God in the flesh because Scripture reveals that He shares the very nature of God while also being sent by the Father. The Bible teaches that “the Word was God” and that this Word “became flesh,” referring to Jesus entering the world as a man (see Gospel of John 1:1,14). At the same time, Jesus is called the Son of God, which describes His relationship with the Father within the divine nature, not that He was created like a human son. Christians understand this through the doctrine of the Trinity: one God who exists eternally as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Thus, Jesus is fully divine yet personally distinct as the Son who reveals the Father to the world.

Jesus came not only to reveal God but to redeem humanity from sin. According to the Bible, all people fall short of God’s holiness and cannot restore themselves to Him (see Epistle to the Romans 3:23). Out of love, God sent Jesus to live a sinless life and die on the cross so that the penalty of sin could be paid on behalf of humanity. Through His resurrection, Jesus demonstrated victory over sin and death, offering forgiveness and eternal life to those who place their faith in Him. Salvation, therefore, is not earned by human effort but received as a gift of grace through Christ.

The concept of hell in Christian teaching flows from God’s justice and human freedom. God is perfectly holy and just, and evil cannot remain in His presence. Yet God also grants humanity the freedom to accept or reject Him. Scripture teaches that those who receive Christ are reconciled to God and given eternal life, while those who reject His grace remain separated from Him (see Gospel of John 3:16–18). Hell, therefore, is understood not as God’s desire for people but as the consequence of rejecting the salvation He lovingly offers through Jesus Christ.
